historical_claims.anchor: In the hours after Mount St. Helens erupted on May eighteenth, 1980, large stretches of the surrounding landscape looked as though nothing living could remain.
Research by Frederick Swanson, Jon Major, Charles Crisafulli, and others emphasized these differences.
The United States Forest Service's long-term work at Mount St. Helens found that plants, animals, and fungi survived across many disturbed areas.
Prairie lupines became important early colonists on nutrient-poor deposits.
The fires in Greater Yellowstone during 1988 provide a different kind of test.
Some lodgepole pines produce serotinous cones, whose scales remain sealed until sufficient heat softens the resin and seeds are released.
Crawford Stanley Holling's 1973 work helped draw an important distinction between the stability of a quantity and the resilience of a system.
In an experiment published in 2011, Stephen Carpenter and colleagues gradually added top predators to a lake over three years while monitoring a nearby reference lake.
Two dams built in the early twentieth century blocked fish migration and altered sediment movement.
US Geological Survey and NOAA monitoring documented fish reaching upstream areas that had been inaccessible for many decades.
A study published in 2026 examined nine years of benthic invertebrate data from different Elwha reaches.
A study of the Elwha delta found that deposition expanded surfaces available for vegetation and that plants gradually colonized them.

description: Examines surviving biological legacies, colonization, succession, Yellowstone fires, Mount St. Helens, lake regime shifts, river restoration, and the difference between recovery and return.
places: Mount St. Helens, Washington, United States
